source.title: 23WSC318 Tutorial: C++ basics (pointers and structures), Loughborough University
source.note: 4 questions (Q4 has parts b, c, d). No official answer sheet. Some boxes hold the student's own answers: Q1, Q2 (main only), Q3 (output only), Q4 (code) and Q4d. Those are claims, checked below against the compiler.

platform: Facts that depend on the platform (sizeof(std::string), short-string capacity) were measured with Apple clang 21 / libc++ on arm64 and are stated with that platform in the game.

concepts.title: Dereferencing a null pointer crashes; assigning null does not
p = &i makes p hold i's address
Call by value works on a copy
A reference is another name for the caller's variable
A pointer parameter lets the function write through to the caller
new T(6) is one T holding 6; new T[6] is six Ts
Out-of-bounds writes, redefinition, leaks and delete[]
A pointer to a struct holds an address; -> follows it
Members are aligned; the compiler inserts padding
std::string has a fixed size; long text lives in a separate heap block
char arrays store text inline, fixed size, and can overflow

misconceptions.text: uint32_t* p = 0; is the line that crashes.
Assigning to a by-value parameter changes the caller's variable.
new uint32_t(6) allocates six uint32_t values.
A House* holds a copy of the House.
sizeof(House) is the sum of its members: 4 + 24 = 28.
A House holding a longer postcode is a bigger House.
Fixed-size char arrays avoid overflow (the student's own Q4d answer).

claims.why: Counting from #include, line 9 is *p = 12;, the first dereference of the null pointer. The process dies there with SIGSEGV.
With p = &i; (plus the semicolon) the program prints 12.

claims.claim: cin >> num1; … AddNumbers(Num1, Num2, &Num3); cout << … Num3
claims.why: The call and the display are right. num1 is not Num1 (C++ is case-sensitive) and the sheet's skeleton has no using namespace std;, so cin/cout/endl need std::. clang reports the errors.
*c = a + b + *c; is the line that stores the answer through the pointer.
Two compile errors: pHeap is defined twice, and *pHeap[3] applies * to a uint32_t.
Compiles and prints Alice Wonderland, 1, 32 bytes per House, addresses 0x20 apart.

claims.claim: char arrays guarantee a fixed size and therefore avoid overflow
claims.why: Fixed size and no hidden heap allocation are real advantages on a microcontroller. But fixed arrays are where overflow happens: strcpy into a char[12] runs straight past the end (AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow). std::string never overflows; its cost is heap allocation that can fail or fragment.
